Question 1: LDA

Let’s start by estimating the components of LDA. From the lecture notes, for each target point 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_0, we find the class label kk with the largest score

𝐱0𝖳𝚺−1𝛍k−12𝛍k𝖳𝚺−1𝛍k+logπk. \mathbf{x}_0^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_k -\frac12\boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_k +\log\pi_k.

Thus, we need to estimate:

  • the prior probabilities πk\pi_k;
  • the mean vector (centroid) 𝛍k\boldsymbol{\mu}_k for each class; and
  • the pooled covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}.

Use saheart.csv, the SAheart data from ElemStatLearn. The two classes are defined by chd, the coronary heart disease indicator. Use all nine other variables as numerical predictors, coding famhist as 1 for Absent and 2 for Present. The following code constructs an n×9n\times9 predictor matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X} and an nn-entry response vector 𝐲\mathbf{y}, where nn is the number of observations.

  • R
  • Python
heart <- read.csv("data/saheart.csv")
heart$famhist <- factor(heart$famhist, levels = c("Absent", "Present"))
X <- data.matrix(heart[, names(heart) != "chd"])
y <- heart$chd
import pandas as pd

heart["famhist"] = heart["famhist"].map({"Absent": 1, "Present": 2})
X = heart.drop(columns="chd").to_numpy()

Provide the confusion matrix, with observed classes in rows and predicted classes in columns. Check that the dimensions of your matrices and vectors match. Calculate the scores yourself for this part.

  3. Perform the same LDA analysis using MASS::lda in R or LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(solver="svd") in Python, using the same numerical predictors and empirical class priors. Provide the confusion matrix. Do the results match?

Solution: Question One

heart$famhist <- factor(heart$famhist,

y <- heart$chd

priors <- prop.table(table(y))

n <- nrow(X)
K <- length(unique(y))

pooled_cov <- matrix(0, ncol(X), ncol(X))

for (k in sort(unique(y))) {
  Xk <- X[y == k, , drop = FALSE]
  pooled_cov <- pooled_cov +
    (nrow(Xk) - 1) * cov(Xk)
}

pooled_cov <- pooled_cov / (n - K)

inv_cov <- solve(pooled_cov)

lda_scores <- sapply(1:2, function(k) {
  mu <- as.numeric(class_means[k, ])
  
  as.vector(X %*% inv_cov %*% mu) -
    0.5 * as.numeric(t(mu) %*% inv_cov %*% mu) +
    log(as.numeric(priors[k]))
})

lda_pred <- max.col(lda_scores) - 1

The estimated prior probabilities are 0.6537 for CHD = 0 and 0.3463 for CHD = 1. The class mean vectors and pooled covariance matrix are shown in the output above.

Using the LDA discriminant scores, the model correctly classified 345 of the 462 observations and incorrectly classified 117. This gives a training misclassification rate of 0.2532, or approximately 25.32%.

The predictions from MASS::lda() exactly matched those from the manual LDA implementation in Question 1(b). Both methods produced the same confusion matrix and training misclassification rate of 0.2532 (25.32%).

Question 2: QDA and marginal screening

In the lecture, ordinary QDA could not be fitted to the handwritten digit sample because its within-class covariance matrices were singular. Let’s consider selecting fewer variables and see whether this helps. For this question, use the full zip-train.csv.gz as the training data and zip-test.csv.gz as the test data, with all ten digit classes. These are the original zip.train and zip.test data from ElemStatLearn. Each file has no header: the first column is the digit label and the remaining 256 columns are pixel values.

Instead of using all 256 predictors, select the 40 with the largest marginal variances in the training data. Here, marginal variance means the variance of one pixel across all training observations. Use the original pixel values without standardizing them, and retain the same selected predictors in the test data.

Use MASS::qda in R or QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(tol=1e-8) in Python.

  1. Fit QDA using these 40 predictors and report the test confusion matrix, with observed classes in rows and predicted classes in columns. Also report the test misclassification rate.

  2. Does the method work? Why do you think it works or does not work?

  3. Repeat the analysis using the 10 predictors with the largest marginal variances in the training data. How does the test misclassification rate compare with the 40-predictor version? Why do you think this happens?

Solution: Question Two

zip_train <- read.csv("data/zip-train.csv.gz", header = FALSE)
zip_test <- read.csv("data/zip-test.csv.gz", header = FALSE)

y_test <- factor(zip_test[[1]], levels = 0:9)

x_train <- as.matrix(zip_train[, -1])
x_test <- as.matrix(zip_test[, -1])

pixel_vars <- apply(x_train, 2, var)
top40 <- order(pixel_vars, decreasing = TRUE)[1:40]

qda40 <- qda(x = x_train[, top40, drop = FALSE],
             grouping = y_train)

pred40 <- predict(qda40, x_test[, top40, drop = FALSE])$class

Using QDA with the 40 highest-variance pixels selected from the training data, the model had a test misclassification rate of 0.1555, or approximately 15.55%. This corresponds to a test classification accuracy of 84.45%.

QDA works with the 40 selected predictors, producing a test misclassification rate of 0.1555 (15.55%). This is because reducing the number of predictors from 256 to 40 helps avoid the singular covariance matrix problem that prevented QDA from working with all 256 pixels. With fewer predictors, QDA can estimate and invert the covariance matrices for each class.

The QDA model using 10 pixels had a test misclassification rate of 0.3423 (34.23%), compared with 0.1555 (15.55%) for the model using 40 pixels. Therefore, the model with 40 pixels performed substantially better on the test data. This suggests that the additional pixels provided useful information for classifying the handwritten digits, while using only 10 pixels removed information that helped distinguish between classes.

Question 3: Compare LDA and QDA

In this simulation, we will study how the relative performance of LDA and QDA changes with the true covariance structure. The parameter ρ\rho controls the distribution from which we generate the data; it is not a tuning parameter of LDA or QDA.

Consider a classification problem with two equally likely classes, labeled 1 and 2, and p=10p=10 covariates. The first two covariates have the class-conditional distributions

(X1X2)∣Y=1∼N2((−10),(1ρρ1)), \begin{pmatrix}X_1\\X_2\end{pmatrix}\mid Y=1 \sim N_2\left( \begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix} \right),

(X1X2)∣Y=2∼N2((10),(1−ρ−ρ1)). \begin{pmatrix}X_1\\X_2\end{pmatrix}\mid Y=2 \sim N_2\left( \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}1&-\rho\\-\rho&1\end{pmatrix} \right).

In both classes, the remaining eight covariates are independent standard normal variables, independent of the first two. Consider

ρ∈{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9}. \rho\in\{0,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9\}.

For each value of ρ\rho, generate 100 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations from each class. Fit ordinary LDA and QDA using all 10 covariates and equal class priors. Estimate the class means from the training data, with one pooled covariance matrix for LDA and one full covariance matrix per class for QDA. Set a random seed and report it.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of ρ\rho. Fit both methods and calculate their test misclassification rates. Within each setting, use the same training and test observations for the two methods.

  2. At each fixed value of ρ\rho, repeat the experiment 50 times, generating new training and test observations in each repetition. Plot average test error against ρ\rho in one figure, with one curve for LDA and one for QDA. These curves compare performance across different data-generating distributions.

  3. Compare the two methods at small and large values of ρ\rho. How does changing the true covariance structure affect their relative performance? Explain the pattern using their covariance assumptions and the bias-variance trade-off. How can the eight noise covariates affect performance even though they contain no information about the class label?

Solution: Question Three

set.seed(432)
rho_values <- c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9)

generate_data <- function(rho, n_per_class) {
  cov1 <- matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2, 2)
  cov2 <- matrix(c(1, -rho, -rho, 1), 2, 2)

  x1 <- cbind(
    mvrnorm(n_per_class, c(-1, 0), cov1),
    matrix(rnorm(n_per_class * 8), ncol = 8)
  )

  x2 <- cbind(
    mvrnorm(n_per_class, c(1, 0), cov2),
    matrix(rnorm(n_per_class * 8), ncol = 8)
  )

  data.frame(
    y = factor(rep(c(1, 2), each = n_per_class)),
    rbind(x1, x2)
  )
}

compare_models <- function(rho) {
  train <- generate_data(rho, 100)
  test <- generate_data(rho, 1000)

lda_fit <- lda(y ~ ., data = train, prior = c(0.5, 0.5))
qda_fit <- qda(y ~ ., data = train, prior = c(0.5, 0.5))

lda_pred <- predict(lda_fit, test)$class
qda_pred <- predict(qda_fit, test)$class

c(
    LDA = mean(lda_pred != test$y),
    QDA = mean(qda_pred != test$y)
  )
}

results_3a <- t(sapply(rho_values, compare_models))

data.frame(
  rho = rho_values,
  LDA_Error = results_3a[, "LDA"],
  QDA_Error = results_3a[, "QDA"]
)
  rho LDA_Error QDA_Error
1 0.0    0.1655    0.1820
2 0.2    0.1585    0.1645
3 0.4    0.1650    0.2000
4 0.6    0.1805    0.1775
5 0.8    0.1640    0.1335
6 0.9    0.1770    0.0970
set.seed(432)

avg_errors <- t(sapply(rho_values, function(rho) {
  errors <- replicate(50, compare_models(rho))
  rowMeans(errors)
}))

avg_results <- data.frame(
  rho = rho_values,
  LDA = avg_errors[, "LDA"],
  QDA = avg_errors[, "QDA"]
)

print(avg_results)
  rho     LDA     QDA
1 0.0 0.17031 0.19823
2 0.2 0.17247 0.19736
3 0.4 0.16895 0.18838
4 0.6 0.16978 0.17460
5 0.8 0.16784 0.13484
6 0.9 0.16793 0.10048
plot(avg_results$rho, avg_results$LDA,
     type = "b", pch = 16, col = "blue",
     ylim = range(avg_results[, c("LDA", "QDA")]),
     xlab = expression(rho),
     ylab = "Average Test Misclassification Rate",
     main = "LDA vs. QDA: Average Test Error")

lines(avg_results$rho, avg_results$QDA,
      type = "b", pch = 17, col = "red")

legend("topright",
       legend = c("LDA", "QDA"),
       col = c("blue", "red"),
       pch = c(16, 17), lty = 1)

The results show that LDA generally had a lower test misclassification rate when the correlation was small, while QDA performed better as the correlation increased. At ρ\rho = 0, LDA had a test error of 0.1655 compared with 0.1820 for QDA. However, at ρ\rho = 0.9, QDA had a much lower test error of 0.0970 compared with 0.1770 for LDA. This makes sense because QDA allows the two classes to have different covariance matrices, while LDA assumes that they share the same covariance matrix.

After repeating the simulation 50 times for each value of ρ\rho, LDA’s average test misclassification rate remained relatively constant at around 0.17. In contrast, QDA’s average test error decreased as ρ\rho increased, going from 0.1982 at ρ\rho = 0 to 0.1005 at ρ\rho = 0.9. LDA performed better at smaller values of ρ\rho, while QDA performed substantially better at larger values of ρ\rho.

  1. When ρ\rho is small, LDA generally performs better because the covariance matrices of the two classes are similar. LDA assumes that the classes share the same covariance matrix, so it estimates fewer parameters than QDA. This reduces variance and can improve prediction performance. QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix for each class, which can increase variance without providing much benefit when the true covariance matrices are similar.

As ρ\rho increases, the covariance matrices of the two classes become more different. LDA’s shared covariance assumption becomes less appropriate, introducing more bias, while QDA can account for these differences using separate covariance matrices. This explains why QDA performs substantially better at larger values of ρ\rho.

The eight noise predictors contain no information about the class labels, but both methods still estimate their means and covariance relationships. This adds unnecessary parameters and estimation variability, potentially increasing prediction error, especially for QDA because it estimates separate covariance matrices for each class.

  1. Define the skill. Write a single SKILL.md file no larger than 5 KB (5,000 bytes). Define the agent’s behavior, analysis guidelines, and expected report structure. Keep the skill independent of this question: provide the dataset, response, and predictors separately when invoking it. The skill may guide the agent to explore lower-dimensional representations, such as principal component analysis (PCA), or to blend the class probabilities predicted by LDA and QDA. Keep all classifiers based on LDA, QDA, or their combination. Configure the skill to load only when you explicitly invoke it. Use your AI tool’s invocation settings, or keep the file outside automatically loaded skill folders and supply it only in an explicit request.

All instructions in the skill must be independent of the actual dataset, its variable names, and its observed results. The report should briefly describe the candidate models, the cross-validation procedure and results, the selected model, and its estimated prediction error. It should explain the main findings and any limitations.

Ask the agent to seek the best predictive performance within the LDA/QDA methods allowed by your skill. Include ordinary LDA and QDA as comparisons; the extensions above are optional. Reserve a test set before choosing models. Use the same cross-validation folds within the training data to compare candidates and select any settings. Estimate any preprocessing, including an embedding, using only the training observations in each fold. Refit the selected model and preprocessing on all training observations, then evaluate the fitted classifier once on the reserved test set. Use misclassification rate to compare performance, and report your random seed.

  2. Review and submit. Check the agent’s analysis and make any skill revisions using only training and cross-validation results. Append the final one-page analysis report and the complete contents of your SKILL.md to your homework report. The one-page limit applies to the analysis report; the appended skill and this explanation are outside that limit.

Solution: Question Four

One-Page LDA/QDA Analysis Report

Answer to Question 4(b)

I explicitly invoked the LDA/QDA Classification Analysis skill in SKILL.md. Complete reproducible R code is in q4b-lda-qda-analysis.R, and the separately rendered one-page report is q4b-report.pdf.

The response was chd; all nine other variables were predictors, with famhist coded 1 for Absent and 2 for Present. There were 462 complete cases (302 class 0, 160 class 1), so no rows or features were excluded. Using seed 43207, I made a stratified 70/30 split: 323 training observations (211/112 by class) and 139 held-out test observations (91/48). I compared candidates on identical stratified five-fold splits of the training set. All scaling and PCA transformations were refitted inside each analysis fold, and all model fits succeeded.

Candidate Selected setting Mean CV misclassification
PCA-LDA 7 PCs 0.257
PCA-QDA 7 PCs 0.261
LDA/QDA probability blend 0.8pLDA+0.2pQDA0.8p_{LDA}+0.2p_{QDA} 0.270
Ordinary LDA all 9 predictors 0.279
Ordinary QDA all 9 predictors 0.288

The minimum CV error selected PCA-LDA with 7 components. After refitting that pipeline to all training observations, I evaluated it once on the reserved test set. Its test misclassification rate was 0.252 (35/139). The confusion matrix, with observed classes in rows and predictions in columns, was:

observed / predicted 0 1
0 75 16
1 19 29

The selected model correctly classified 104/139 observations; class-1 sensitivity was 0.604 and specificity was 0.824. PCA likely helped by reducing covariance-estimation variance, but this conclusion is conditional on one moderately sized, imbalanced split. PCA is outcome-blind, the 0.5 cutoff was not tuned, and test-error uncertainty is substantial, so these results do not establish universal superiority.

I reviewed the agent’s analysis and checked that it followed the instructions in my skill. The agent compared ordinary LDA and QDA with PCA-based models and an LDA/QDA probability blend. It used the same five cross-validation folds for all candidates and performed preprocessing within each training fold. PCA-LDA with seven principal components had the lowest mean cross-validation misclassification rate of 0.257. After refitting the selected model on the training data, the agent evaluated it on the reserved test set and obtained a misclassification rate of 0.252. I did not make any revisions to the skill.

My SKILL.md file is 2,683 bytes, below the 5,000-byte limit. I saved it at homework/week-07/SKILL.md, outside the automatically loaded skill directories. This allowed me to explicitly invoke the skill by directing my AI agent to read that specific file.

Complete contents of SKILL.md:

---
name: LDA/QDA Classification Analysis
description: Build and evaluate reproducible classification models using ordinary LDA and QDA, and choose a model by training-only cross-validation.
---

# LDA/QDA Classification Analysis

1. Check response labels, predictor types, missing values, class counts, and whether covariance estimates are feasible. Explain any excluded rows or features. Never use outcome information to preprocess predictors.
2. Set and report a random seed. Make a stratified train/test split before model comparison. Hold the test set untouched until the final model has been selected. Use an approximately 70/30 split unless the user specifies otherwise.
3. Compare ordinary LDA and QDA as mandatory candidates. If QDA has singular within-class covariance matrices, document this and use an appropriate training-only feature reduction or PCA-QDA candidate; do not silently omit QDA. Additional candidates are optional.
4. Use identical stratified cross-validation folds for all candidates within the training data (default: 5 folds). Refit every preprocessing step, including imputation, scaling, feature selection, and PCA, within each training fold. Apply those fitted steps to that fold's validation data. Never select settings using test data.
5. Calculate fold-level misclassification rates; compare candidates by mean validation error, breaking ties in favor of the simpler model. Report CV mean errors and the selected settings. If a model fails on a fold, record the failure rather than replacing it with an invented score.
6. Refit the selected pipeline on the entire training set. Predict the reserved test set exactly once. Report test misclassification rate, test sample size, and confusion matrix. Distinguish CV selection results from final held-out evaluation.
7. Check for class imbalance, small class sample sizes, covariance instability, and uncertainty from one split. Avoid claims of universal superiority.

Create a legible statistical report of **at most one printed page**. Include: a short data/split description and random seed; a compact table of candidate models, CV mean misclassification rates, and selected settings; one clearly labeled figure showing comparative CV performance; the selected model; held-out test misclassification rate and numerical model-fitting results; and a brief interpretation with limitations. A small confusion matrix may be included if space permits. Keep tables and plots readable when printed. Supply reproducible code separately from the one-page report when requested.
